title: Mechanisms and vulnerabilities of ERG-driven luminal fate in prostate cancer
text:
The ERG oncoprotein is responsible for half cases of prostate cancer, the most frequent cancer and the
second leading cause of cancer death among American men. Prostate cancer features a luminal cell identity
which is effectively targeted by hormone therapy, but resistance invariably occurs, thus demanding a deeper
understanding of the biology underlying the cancer cell identity. This proposal seeks to elucidate the
mechanisms and vulnerabilities of ERG-driven luminal cell identity during prostate cancer formation, the
completion of which may reveal new treatment paradigms.

title: Biospecimens and Neuroimaging Core
text: BIOSPECIMENS AND NEUROIMAGING CORE - ABSTRACT The biomarker landscape in Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (AD/ADRD) has rapidly advanced, driven by initiatives like the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, positron emission tomography (PET) tracers, and fluid biomarker assays. Plasma-based markers such as phosphorylated tau (p-tau217) and amyloid beta (Aβ42/40 ratio) have shown considerable promise in early detection of AD pathology, yet more work is needed to advance MRI technology in the brain in parallel with blood-based markers. At the 1Florida Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (ADRC), innovations such as free-water imaging reveal biological changes in the cortex and subcortex even in amyloid PET-negative but blood-positive cases, suggesting earlier MRI detection than previously thought. The Biomarker and Neuroimaging (BN) Core at 1Florida ADRC prioritizes both established and novel biomarkers to advance early detection, trial enrichment, prognosis, treatment monitoring, and precision medicine. Key innovations under study include: Imaging and machine learning tools such as Automated Imaging Differentiation for Dementia (AIDD) and Automated Neurodegeneration Index (ANDI), Cognitive assessments including the Loewenstein-Acevedo Scales for Semantic Interference and Learning (LASSI-L), and Biofluid assays such as new tau antibody-based Simoa assays. The BN Core has been highly productive, publishing in leading journals, developing patents in imaging, enabling multiple NIH-funded grants, training junior researchers, and creating secure platforms for data sharing across the University of Florida, University of Miami, and Mt. Sinai Medical Center. The renewal has four main aims. 1) Standardized Biomarker Collection and Sharing that will leverage harmonized biofluid and imaging protocols across sites. 2) Evaluation of Novel Cognitive and Imaging Markers for predicting cognitive decline and building on patented free-water imaging and machine learning approaches. 3) Development of New Biofluid Markers including NULISA biomarkers and evaluate Florida-developed tau antibodies in human samples to improve sensitivity and specificity for early detection and tracking. 4) Support for Training and Grants by providing infrastructure for multimodal analyses, biofluid assays, and national data-sharing, while fostering public/private partnerships and supporting state and national grants (R01, U01, K, F, T32, etc.). Through these efforts, the 1Florida ADRC BN Core aims to advance biomarker science, support clinical trials, and enable precision approaches in AD/ADRD research.

title: An Integrated Neurochemical/Electrophysiological Recording and Neuromodulation System for Basic and Clinical Research
text:
The proposed studies consist of three Aims in which, in Aim 1, WINCS International LLC, in partnership with
Mayo Clinic Neural Engineering Laboratories and Division of Engineering, will finalize the development of a
novel neurochemical/electrophysiological recording and stimulating instrument, called Multifunctional
Apparatus for Voltammetry, Electrophysiology and Neuromodulation (MAVEN), together with a sophisticated
user-friendly software interface, for a broad range of clinical neuroscience research in subjects undergoing
intraoperative brain neurosurgeries. In Aim 2, overall development and construction plans for the MAVEN
system will ensure that device manufacturing processes and design history files meet regulatory Design
Control and medical safety requirements necessary to obtain approval for an FDA Investigational Device
Exemption (IDE). Aim 3 is designed to integrate several MAVEN recording protocols into existing intraoperative
clinical neurosurgical procedures (e.g., deep brain stimulation neurosurgeries and cortical lobectomies) using a
large animal model (swine), including confirming MAVEN’s ability to reliably record neurochemical and
electrophysiological events (e.g., dopamine, serotonin, and adenosine, and action/local field potential activity,
respectively) for future use of the system in IDE-enabled mechanistic clinical studies.

title: Genomic Conflict Resolution: Establishment of a new model for unconstrained germline selection
text:
Germline selection and somatic conflict describe how beneficial de novo mutations in reproductive cells can
“selfishly” result in spontaneous congenital disorders for offspring, often occurring in complex and ill-defined
ways that confound proper diagnosis. This proposal will explore these genomic conflicts using the germline
restricted chromosome of songbirds, which uniquely isolates germline selective pressures in gene duplications
through their programmed DNA elimination from somatic tissues. The establishment of a novel zebra finch model
to study this chromosome will provide a bird’s eye view of germline sequence flexibility that underlies heritable
mutations and spontaneous congenital disorders.

title: TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION OF BEIGE ADIPOCYTE CELLULAR PLASTICITY
text: Beige fat cells can consume a large quantity of calories as heat and hold great promise for combating the epidemic of obesity and metabolic disorders. This project will explore a new pathway of beige adipocyte generation, its regulation by a gene called NFIL3, and its effect on whole body energy balance and glucose control. This study will suggest new ways to treat and/or prevent obesity, diabetes and other metabolic diseases.

title: Targeting T Cells for enhancing anti-tumor immunity in pediatric brain tumors.
text:
Brain tumors are the most common solid tumors in children, and outcomes remain poor for a
significant proportion of patients despite aggressive multimodal therapy. Brain tumors are
understudied and considered to be immunologically-silent, however we show striking clonal
expansion of tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells with a transcriptional program supportive of effector
function, tissue-residency, PD-1 expression and neoantigen specificity. The proposed study will
determine the prevalence, transcriptional properties and in vivo function of neoantigen-specific
CD8+ T cells in an ethnically-diverse patient cohort with pediatric brain tumors (medulloblastoma
and pediatric high-grade glioma) using single-cell RNA sequencing, TCR sequencing, TCR
engineering and patient-derived xenograft models; translation of these findings will lead to clinical
trial testing neoantigen-based immunotherapy in childhood brain tumors.

title: Wastewater-Based Microbial Genomics to Enhance Surveillance for Foodborne Pathogens
text:
Overall
Project Narrative
Whole genome sequencing (WGS) is the gold standard for tracking the spread of human pathogens in foods
and the environment. This project describes the continued collaboration between Penn State and the
Pennsylvania Department of Health, to generate WGS data and to develop an efficient pipeline that can
identify foodborne pathogens circulating in communities, using existing wastewater-based surveillance
infrastructure.

title: Viral MEM: Viral Enrichment and Precise Stochastic Quantification with Microbial Context Preservation for Rigorous Virome Analysis of Challenging Human Samples
text:
This U01 proposal aims to advance the Human Virome Project by developing and validating innovative
technologies that address critical challenges in virome analysis, especially in human tissue samples. Our focus
is on the development of Viral-MEM and Viral StochQuant, which are designed to enrich viromes, preserve
microbial context, and enhance the accuracy and reproducibility of viral sequencing. These advancements may
significantly improve our understanding of the human virome and its interactions with the immune system and
the rest of the microbiome, paving the way for new diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.

title: Harvard-wide Program on Antibiotic Resistance
text:
The Harvard-wide Program on Antibiotic Resistance is designed to fill critical gaps in knowledge
that will allow new approaches for treating serious infections with antibiotic resistant staphylococci
and enterococci to be developed. This is done by identifying and where needed, creating new
advanced technologies to gain insight into how these microbes can be targeted by new classes
of molecules, and by more thoroughly understanding how they survive treatment with current
antibiotics. These critical advances are accomplished through synergistic interaction among a
multidisciplinary team ranging in expertise from mathematics to infectious diseases, with each
sharing their special insight and working together to achieve goals that otherwise would be
unattainable.

title: Epigenetic Regulation of Microglial Identity and Function by ARID5B in Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Alzheimer’s disease is a devastating condition marked by cognitive decline and chronic neuroinflammation,
with microglial dysfunction playing a central role in its progression. Epigenetic changes, including modifications
to histone marks like H3K9me2 and H3K9ac, are thought to drive shifts in microglial behavior toward disease-
associated states. This proposal focuses on understanding how the epigenetic modification regulator ARID5B
shapes microglial function in Alzheimer’s, using CRISPR models and multi-omics profiling to identify pathways
that could guide new therapeutic strategies.

title: Immunotherapy for Glioblastoma by Targeting an Immunoregulatory Neuropeptide
text:
This proposal uncovers a novel pathogenic axis in which glioblastoma co-opts trigeminal sensory neurons to
promote immune evasion via calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)–mediated reprogramming of tumor-
associated macrophages and subsequent suppression of anti-GBM CD8⁺ T cell function. We demonstrate that
targeting this neuroimmune pathway boosts antitumor immunity and sensitizes glioblastoma to immune
checkpoint blockade. These findings provide a strong mechanistic rationale for repurposing FDA-approved drugs
that target trigeminal sensory neurons and their downstream pathways, offering a promising and urgently needed
therapeutic strategy for this intractable disease.

title: Post-transcriptional regulation by RNA binding proteins in liver fibrosis
text:
Chronic liver injury leads to fibrosis, driven by the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) and excessive
production of fibrotic proteins. This proposal investigates the role of the RNA binding protein LARP6 in regulating
fibrosis-related genes, promoting collagen production, and inducing liver fibrosis. By uncovering the molecular
mechanisms behind LARP6’s activity and exploring targeted therapies, we aim to develop new strategies to treat
liver fibrosis.

title: Foundations for Next-Generation Intrapartum Decision Support via Fusion of Selective State-Space Models
text:
This project will provide clinicians and expectant parents with real-time, explainable AI methods that rec-
ognize fetal distress earlier, reduce preventable complications, and improve birth outcomes for mothers and
newborns.

title: Data Management and Statistical Core
text: ABSTRACT- DATA MANAGEMENT & STATISTICS CORE (DMSC) The Data Management and Statistical Core (DMSC) supports the NYU Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (ADRC) and its Cores by providing state-of-the-art data and information management and statistical expertise. The DMS Core aims to maintain a robust data infrastructure and enhance data management and integration (AIM 1). We will continue to develop an integrated data management system in REDCap supporting multimodal data collection, storage and analysis of data in a secure, scalable format, while complying to institutional and industry standards, and refine electronic data acquisition tools, incorporating open-source tools, machine learning, and artificial intelligence to improve automated data capture methods while ensuring data quality and integrity using strict data collection protocols and rigorous validation processes. The DMSC aims to enhance analytical capabilities to support innovative research and improve data sharing and accessibility using compliant systems through ethical data management practices (AIM 2). We will continue to enhance data analytics capabilities to provide statistical, bioinformatics, machine-learning, and computational support data driven studies with real-time data analysis capabilities; and facilitate broad data sharing within the scientific community by adhering to NIH Genomic Data Sharing Policy and to ensure interoperability and data standardization between national repositories like NACC and other National centralized repositories and consortiums and collaborator like the Diverse Vascular Contributions to Cognitive Impairment and Dementia (VCID) allowing for collaborative research and regular data transfers. Furthermore, we will promote the use of interoperable standard to help gain access to “real-life” or real-world data by interfacing with other databases and exchanges to help develop predictive models that would aid in reducing research bias. The DMSC aims to provide state-of-the-art statistical collaboration/consultation to all ADRC cores and training/mentoring to young investigators and trainees (AIM3). We offer comprehensive statistical collaboration and consultation to all ADRC research projects, and provide support on study design, data analysis, and interpretation of findings to ensure scientific rigor and reproducibility. We will continue to provide training and mentoring on study design, data collection, management, and statistical analysis methods to ADRC researchers, including trainees from REC and other affiliated programs, promoting skill development in statistics, informatics and data-analytics, across the research community. The DMSC aims to develop innovative statistical methods and novel study designs to address specific needs arising in research by NYU ADRC investigators (AIM4). We will continue to develop and implement innovative statistical methods, bioinformatics tools, and machine learning algorithms to address specific analytic needs arising in research undertaken by ADRC investigators including development of novel clinical trial designs and sampling strategies with open platform R packages to share with ADRD researchers free of charge.

title: Understanding and Targeting Aberrant RNA Splicing in Leukemia
text:
For the past 13 years my lab has sought to understand both the genetic basis of hematopoietic malignancies
and the mechanisms through which mutations in splicing factors mediate oncogenesis. This R35 award would
enable my laboratory to focus on identifying the mechanisms by which mutations in the RNA splicing
machinery drive the development of a wide range of myeloid and lymphoid leukemias and develop novel
therapies for leukemias driven by these mutations. This research is significant as gain-of-function mutations in
RNA splicing factors are the single most common class of genetic alterations in patients with myelodysplastic
syndrome (MDS) and, as such, developing means to target gain-of-function mutations present in >50% of such
patients would be transformative.

title: Cyclin C-CDK8/19 kinases in development and in cancer
text:
Cyclin C-CDK8 and C-CDK19 kinases were implicated to perform cancer-promoting functions. This proposal
will examine the molecular roles played by these proteins in promoting cancer growth, acting within the host
immune system, and the utility of inhibiting these proteins in cancer treatment.

title: Biomedical Engineering Core
text: Precision Medicine (PM) is revolutionizing the care of patients by tailoring treatment options based on the molecular composition of their disease. To secure the necessary molecular information, liquid biopsies represent an exciting source of molecular markers because of the minimally invasive nature of securing them, the plethora of marker types (circulating biological cells, cell-free molecules [proteins, micro-RNA, cell-free DNA] and extracellular vesicles [exosomes]), and the extensive molecular information they carry. The challenge with the use of these exciting markers is that the disease-associated liquid biopsy markers can be a vastly lower in abundance compared to other entities found in a clinical sample making it difficult to secure high-quality results. This is partly due to a lack of platforms for their efficient isolation and tools to analyze the limited numbers of diseased molecules contained in a liquid biopsy isolate. The use of microfluidics has become a valuable platform technology to generate high quality isolates that can be fed into molecular analysis technologies such as NGS to secure results to guide treatment decisions in the clinic (i.e., translational research) as well as driving basic discoveries. The KIPM COBRE’s Biomedical Engineering Core (BME Core) is a unique Core within the medical enterprise and consists of two units: (i) Plastics Engineering Unit (PEU); and (ii) Liquid Biopsy Unit (LBU). The PEU has enabling infrastructure built during the Phase 1 funding of KIPM including a state-of-the-art cleanroom with patterning equipment possessing the ability to generate both microstructures and nanostructures and production equipment to support large-scale clinical studies associated with KIPM’s RPLs and outside users. The LBU uses microfluidic devices emanating from the PEU that possess unprecedented figures-of-merit to analyze liquid biopsy markers. The LBU also has liquid handling robots to automate the microfluidic workflow. Both units operated collaboratively to support the Phase 1 junior faculty projects as well as many external projects from the KU community and nationally. The activities of the BME Core and their unique hardware and molecular assays are enabled by collaborations with a P41 NIH National Biotechnology Resource Center, directed by the mPI of KIPM (Soper), and whose mission is to deliver innovative technologies into the biomedical community. In the KIPM Phase 2, the BME Core will seek to add new resource capabilities to both units supporting the RPLs to facilitate their securing funding from different federal agencies. These capabilities include nanopatterning to generate new innovative tools and assays for the analysis of a variety of molecular types, the efficient isolation of cell free DNA to support NGS studies by the RPLs using a unique microfluidic device, and a highly innovative single-molecule sequencing strategy. The BME Core will strive to develop business models to sustain long-term operation, increase visibility to recruit external users, and maintain a seasoned staff. Dissemination of new discoveries will be facilitated through a robust website, meeting participation, and timely publications.

title: Core B: Biospecimen and Pathology Resources Core
text:
All of the proposed SPORE projects are dependent on the pathology and tissue resources provided by the 
Biospecimen and Pathology Resources Core (Core B). The Core B Director is a pathologist with 
histomorphologic and research expertise in adult kidney cancers, and with extensive experience in biobanking. 
The proposed Core infrastructure will further strengthen our ongoing translational mission and has the potential 
to revolutionize personalized medicine in renal cancer.

title: MYBPC1-targeted therapeutic discovery platform for treatment of distal arthrogryposis
text:
Distal arthrogryposis affects 1 in 3,000 live births and currently has no effective drug treatments.
This project aims to develop first-in-class therapies by targeting slow skeletal myosin-binding
protein C (sMyBP-C). Using recombinant biosensors in high-throughput and machine learning-
driven virtual screens, we will identify small molecules for testing in mouse models, advancing a
streamlined path to selective sMyBP-C drugs for this congenital muscle disorder.

title: Examination of potential effectiveness of transcranial direct current stimulation (TDCS) paired with reappraisal training for Cannabis Use Disorder
text:
The goal of this work is to examine if transcranial direct current stimulation (TDCS), paired with training in the
emotional regulation strategy of reappraisal, may enhance regulation of craving (measured with self-report and
EEG) in individuals with Cannabis Use Disorder (CUD) and result in clinical reduction of cannabis use as
measured by ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Sixty participants with CUD will be randomized to
either real or sham DLPFC stimulation in 5 20-minute TDCS and reappraisal training sessions one week apart
using a double-blind design, with EEG sessions at the first and final visit, and participants will report daily
cannabis use with EMA. Findings will serve important proof-of-concept data on the clinical effectiveness of
TDCS as an augment for CUD treatment.
